cells.tense: Right now the pen is in your hand and the adjusting is happening as you go.
cells.act: release what is done and keep what is not
cells.ask: Something you're growing has already reached what you meant it to. Stop working on it, and leave the unfinished ones to your hands.
cells.core:
You can adjust as you go without needing to name it. When something you've been growing reaches what you meant it to be, you can take your hands off it without needing it to thank you — and the moment you do, whatever's still open gets the attention. That's not quitting. It's knowing finished from nearly there and acting on the difference.

There's one in your care that's done. You can feel it when you stop for a second. This week, put it down — nothing further from it, nothing further asked of it — and let what's still forming have the room. Setting a finished thing down is how it's completed, not how it's lost. The floor stays steady. What you keep will grow because the space got quieter.
cells.sheetLine: You can finish something by setting it down.
cells.verb: learning how things grow by tending them, one hand on the soil
cells.place: a place where you keep sensing when to add and when to subtract

cells.tense: You are bracing against a future you can't write in yet, and pushing before it asks.
cells.act: dream the next step and take it
cells.ask: Hands off for ten minutes; picture the version of something you tend that's a step further on, feel toward it, then move one pace — not the plan.
cells.core:
With what you're growing, you're leaning on the next season harder than the one you're in. You read what isn't here yet, you feel toward it before it arrives, and care that used to be patient is now a palm pressed on a stem to make it taller. It wears you down, and the thing being pushed can tell watering from pulling.

Sense the next thing before you move it. Ten minutes, no decisions — picture the version of something you tend that's a step further on, and feel toward it the way you'd feel about something you already understand. Then take one small step, not the plan. Ease comes back through the feeling, not through effort. The picture is the point; trust it enough to walk one pace.
cells.sheetLine: You're pushing a stem to make it taller.

cells.tense: You are still standing at a door that has already closed behind you.
cells.act: start something for the spark of starting
cells.ask: Begin something this week with no purpose past beginning it — a meal you've never made, a sketch, a road you don't know — and don't decide what it's for.
cells.core:
What you're growing has gone quiet in your hands. You water what's already placed, you handle what's familiar, and the open, curious part of how you learn has pulled back. Your hands still work. The wondering has gone home. New things stop getting apprenticed to you because you stopped asking them to.

Start something for the spark of starting, not because it fits anything. A meal you've never made, a sketch, a shelf, a road you don't know. Keep it small and purposeless. You'll know the spark by the feeling of not caring where it lands. That feeling is what opens the door again — it doesn't ask your permission, and it doesn't need a reason.
cells.sheetLine: The wondering has gone home, and you're watering without it.
cells.verb: learning how things grow by tending them, one hand on the soil
cells.place: a place where you keep sensing when to add and when to subtract

cells.tense: You are still writing, and your hand is already down on the page.
cells.act: govern by knowing what to surrender
cells.ask: For a week, choose something you've been holding tightly and take a hand off it — no correcting, no steering — and watch what comes of it.
cells.core:
You grow things, and the growing is steady — you notice when to add, when to subtract, which one wants less, which one wants more. You'd say the things around you just grow that way. But the adjusting is yours; your hand made those choices. It's been filed under circumstance, or under luck. What you've been holding doesn't care what it's called.

For a week, take a hand off the thing you've been holding tightly. Let it come out as it comes out — no correction, no steering — and watch what happens. You aren't abandoning it; you're finding out how much of its growth was your watching. What's finished can be let go of. What you keep stays. You've been governing by knowing what to hand over.

attempts.check: The one claim the record does not support: that the person has kept the thing they tend young on purpose, or that they tend only what they can predict. The record says the signature is tending and learning how things grow; it says nothing about what or whom is being tended, or why. A reader could rightly say 'I don't do this with people' or 'I don't have anything growing.' The ask survives being wrong because it works on any object the person actually tends — a plant, a skill, a task, a room — and the core says where the capacity stands, not what it is for. The line that serves the writer more than the person: any sentence that sounds like the reader should recognise themselves in being an apprentice; I cut those and kept the mechanism plain.
